It states the mitigation module's method in one place; describes the two AI-assisted rebuilds and the 228 legacy bugs they found; gathers the published validation and adds a check of the price elasticities that drive every result; and sets out three extensions that ministries ask for: exposure to the EU carbon border adjustment, the investment and public-spending side of climate policy, and a common activity layer that links CPAT to other models. # A model nobody can audit is a recommendation taken on trust {.unnumbered}

The Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), built by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, estimates what carbon pricing and related policies do to energy use, emissions, revenue, growth and households for more than 180 countries. Ministries use its numbers to set rates and sequence reforms. Until recently almost nobody could check them: the legacy model was a very large Excel workbook, and its 57,000-word mitigation documentation disagreed with the model in places.

The papers in this section make the model legible, check it and extend it. They are written so that an economist can understand each piece in an afternoon, and each points to the code and documentation in the CPAT-AI repository for the detail.

# What the model computes (paper 4.1) {.unnumbered}

The mitigation module is six blocks and about eighteen equations. Retail prices are built up from supply cost, existing taxes, subsidies and the new carbon charge. Fuel use responds through income, usage and efficiency elasticities. An engineering power model dispatches, retires and invests. Emissions and revenue follow by accounting identities, and revenue moves GDP a year later through fiscal multipliers. In the paper's stylized example a \$50 per tonne carbon price cuts industrial coal use by about a third and road fuel use by about 6 percent. The power model also reports investment spending, priced at default costs of capital of 7.5, 10, 12.5 and 15 percent for high-, upper-middle-, lower-middle- and low-income countries. Road transport is the module's weak joint: CPAT describes it three times, in a simple fuel equation, an engineering fleet model and a co-benefits module, and the three are not linked and disagree on how much drivers cut their driving when fuel prices rise (papers 4.1, 4.3 and 4.7 flag this). The paper gives the corrected equation wherever the documentation is wrong and proposes a penalty-based investment rule as an alternative to the logit share rule, which never lets a technology's share reach zero.

# Rebuild it twice (paper 4.2) {.unnumbered}

The model was rebuilt twice in October 2026 with AI coding agents, Claude Code and GitHub Copilot, doing most of the construction: once as a readable Excel workbook generated by code (Excel-AI) and once as a Python model (Coded CPAT) that reproduces it number for number. One rule governed both: errors in the legacy model are fixed and never copied; questionable but intended choices are copied and logged. The rebuild found 228 bugs in the legacy model, 24 of them high priority because they change standard results, together with 135 issues (intended choices open to question), 35 deliberate departures and 20 errors in the documentation. Writing the model a second time found seven more bugs in the first rebuild. The lesson is general: specify a policy model by shared variable codes, build it at least twice and test it at every change.

# Check it against data and other models (papers 4.3 and 4.4) {.unnumbered}

The published validation shows a model good for ranges and policy comparisons, not point forecasts. CPAT reproduces its base year by construction, follows the trend of emissions in back-casts from 2000 for several countries, and gives baselines and carbon-price responses of the same order as other energy models; it fits poorly where prices are hard to forecast, as for China. The rebuilt versions reproduce the legacy blocks to many decimal places. Every published check predates the bug fixes and should be rerun.

The price elasticities matter more than any other input, and most of them pass. Seven of ten fuel-sector defaults lie within the range of published meta-analyses; three are too high, and road gasoline is double the estimate corrected for publication bias. Two structural choices matter more than any single value: the full long-run response is applied within one year, and there are no cross-price terms. Paper 4.4 sets out a protocol for future updates.

# Extend it where policy needs it (papers 4.5 to 4.7) {.unnumbered}

The CBAM Policy Tool measures what the EU carbon border adjustment will cost a country's exporters and how domestic policy changes that. In the public-data example for Turkish hot-rolled steel at €80 per tonne, the charge on goods declared at default values rises from about €107 per tonne in 2026 to €252 at full phase-in; verified emissions data and a €20 domestic carbon price together cut the full charge by two-fifths. The tool's Egypt application shows where emissions data matter most: Egypt has no EU country default for steel, so its gas-based steel would be charged as if it came from the most intensive exporters, and verified data would cut the full-phase-in charge on seven Egyptian exports from about €595 million to €177 million a year (paper 4.5; illustrative tool results, not official estimates).

The public investment extension turns the physical change CPAT computes into investment needs, prices that capital at the rates countries actually pay, and tests whether public money should pay for it. For a stylized clean asset the financial case fails above a 12.6 percent cost of capital, almost exactly the rate CPAT assumes for lower-middle-income countries, which links this section to the de-risking papers in section 2. Country runs put 2030 climate investment needs in Kenya, Uganda and St Lucia at 4 to 5 percent of GDP; in Kenya and Uganda the increment over current trends pays only when cleaner air is counted, while St Lucia's diesel-based power makes it pay at any rate, and a SISEPUEDE run for Uganda shows that under a fifth of its net-zero benefits reach the budget as cash (paper 4.6; illustrative tool results).

The activity extension gives CPAT, SISEPUEDE, the CBAM tool and the Future Technology Transformations models one driver layer for population, income and service costs, mapped through a common sector concordance, so they can be linked without counting a price response twice (paper 4.7).
